title: 'Drinking Alone by Moonlight' (Yuexia duzhuo), no. 1
short: The first of Li Bai's four poems 'Drinking Alone beneath the Moon', in Arthur Waley's 1919 version.
body: Li Bai (701-762) wrote a set of four poems titled 月下獨酌 Yuexia duzhuo, 'Drinking alone beneath the moon'; this is the first, a fourteen-line poem of five characters per line in the old-style (gushi) form, which allows changes of rhyme. Waley printed three of the four under the heading 'Three Poems' in More Translations from the Chinese (1919), translating each Chinese line by one English line with a stress-based rhythm rather than rhyme. Li Bai's reputation as the drinking 'immortal banished from heaven' made such poems central to his legend. Line 1 in Chinese reads 花間一壺酒, 'among flowers, a pot of wine': Waley's 'cup' and 'under the flowering trees' are free renderings, and the Chinese 'pot' (hu, a flask) becomes the cup that is raised in l. 3.

title: drinking alone
short: Drinking was a social rite in Tang China; to drink alone is a sign of isolation, which the poem then playfully overcomes.
body: The Chinese 獨酌無相親 says 'I pour alone, with no one close to me'. Wine-drinking among friends, with toasts, poetry games and music, was the normal setting for Tang poetry, so drinking alone signals estrangement. Li Bai's literary model is Tao Yuanming (365-427), whose twenty 'Drinking Wine' poems also present solitary drinking as a way out of the world's falseness (see the Tao Qian poem in this archive, 'I built my hut in a zone of human habitation'). Li Bai's poem turns loneliness into a comic party with invented companions. Waley's 'for no friend is near' turns the statement into a causal clause.

title: moon, shadow and self make three
short: The poet invites the moon and finds his shadow, so that the three make a drinking party: the poem's famous central conceit.
body: 舉杯邀明月，對影成三人: 'raising my cup I invite the bright moon; facing my shadow, we make three people'. The conceit treats the moon and the shadow cast by moonlight as guests, creating company out of the conditions of solitude. It has a precedent in the Chinese habit of personifying the moon, but the arithmetic joke is Li Bai's own and became proverbial. Waley's 'For he, with my shadow, will make three men' makes the moon masculine, a choice the Chinese, which has no grammatical gender, does not force; in l. 9 he calls it 'her beams', so the moon's gender shifts within the translation. Owen reads the poem as Li Bai's characteristic staging of a self at play.

title: the moon cannot drink
short: The fantasy breaks: the moon cannot drink and the shadow only imitates, so the companions are both present and absent.
body: 月既不解飲，影徒隨我身: 'the moon does not understand drinking; the shadow merely follows my body'. The joke has a philosophical edge: the companions are real only as extensions of the drinker. 徒 tu ('merely, in vain') is Waley's 'Listless', which gives the shadow a mood not quite in the Chinese; 'creeps about at my side' is his vivid gloss on 隨 sui, 'follow'. Waley's 'alas' (l. 5) also adds a sigh absent from the original's matter-of-fact tone.

title: 'the moon as friend and the shadow as slave'
short: Waley's 'friend' and 'slave' interpret a line usually read as 'for now I keep company with the moon and with my shadow'.
body: The Chinese is 暫伴月將影, 'for a while I accompany the moon, together with the shadow'. Most editors take 將 jiang as a connective ('with, and'), so the line simply pairs the two companions. Waley's antithesis of 'friend' and 'slave' seems to draw on other senses of jiang ('to lead, command'), making the shadow a servant who must follow; the variant text 暫伴明月影 ('the bright moon's shadow') shows the line was already unsettled in transmission. Waley also drops 暫 zan, 'for a while', a word that anticipates the parting in l. 12. Students should treat Waley's reading as an interpretation rather than the plain sense.

title: carpe diem: enjoy pleasure while it is spring
short: A Chinese 'seize the day' formula: pleasure must be taken in season, for spring and life are brief.
body: 行樂須及春, 'making merry must catch the spring'. 行樂 'to take one's pleasure' belongs to a long tradition of poems, from the Han 'Nineteen Old Poems' onward, that urge enjoyment because human life is short; the archive holds Giles's version of one such poem as 'Carpe Diem' (classical-chinese-anonymous). Spring here is both the season of the flowers in l. 1 and the prime of life. Waley's 'I must make merry' keeps the obligation in 須 xu, 'must'.

title: parallel couplet: song and dance
greek: 我歌月徘徊，我舞影零亂
short: Lines 9 and 10 are a parallel couplet in the Chinese: 'I sing, the moon lingers; I dance, the shadow scatters.'
body: 我歌月徘徊，我舞影零亂. Each line has the same grammar (I + verb, companion + response), the moon answering the song and the shadow the dance. 徘徊 pai-huai, 'to pace to and fro, linger', suggests the moon wavering or hesitating as if listening, which Waley turns into 'flickers her beams'. 零亂 ling-luan, 'scattered, in disorder', becomes 'tangles and breaks', a good image of a shadow on uneven ground as the drunk man dances. Note that Waley's moon is 'he' in l. 4 and 'her' here; Chinese allows either, and the moon is traditionally yin (feminine) and associated with the goddess Chang'e.

title: sober and drunk
greek: 醒時同交歡，醉後各分散
short: The fellowship holds only while the drinker is sober; drunkenness scatters the party, an ironic reversal of convivial drinking.
body: 醒時同交歡，醉後各分散: 'when sober, we share our joy together; after drunkenness, each goes his way'. The paradox is that drinking, meant to unite, ends the company: the drunk man falls asleep, the moon sets, the shadow vanishes. Waley's 'three shared the fun' is colloquial for 交歡, 'exchange delight'. The couplet also echoes the language of human partings, preparing the final vow of reunion.

title: 'unfeeling' companionship (wuqing you 無情遊)
short: Li Bai vows a lasting friendship 'without feeling': either with things that cannot feel, or in a Daoist freedom from emotion.
body: 永結無情遊, 'forever bind ourselves in a wanderer's friendship without feeling'. 無情 wuqing literally means 'without feelings'. One reading is literal and comic: the moon and shadow are insentient, so this is friendship with things, which Waley renders 'our odd, inanimate feast'. Another reading, favoured by many Chinese commentators, hears a Daoist ideal: a bond beyond ordinary human attachment, free of the passions that make human friendship painful. 遊 you is 'roaming, excursion', a Zhuangzi word for free and easy wandering, which Waley turns into 'feast'. The two senses can coexist, and the line is the poem's turn from play to something like spiritual longing.

anchor: the Cloudy River of the sky
title: Cloudy River (yunhan 雲漢): the Milky Way
short: Waley's own footnote glosses the Cloudy River as the Milky Way, where the friends will meet far off in heaven.
body: 相期邈雲漢, 'we pledge to meet in the far-off Cloudy Han'. 雲漢 yunhan, the 'Cloudy Han River', is an old name for the Milky Way, seen as a heavenly counterpart of the Han River; Waley footnoted the phrase 'The Milky Way'. The word goes back to the Shijing ode 'Yun Han' (Mao 258). The Milky Way is also the river that separates the Weaver Girl and the Cowherd, who meet once a year, so a promised meeting there carries a faint note of lovers' reunion across distance. The final line lifts the poem from tipsy play to a cosmic, almost Daoist, rendezvous with the immortals among whom Li Bai liked to place himself.
